name: Orthodontic retainer
lead: An orthodontic retainer is a custom appliance, either removable (a wire-and-acrylic Hawley or a clear vacuum-formed plastic tray) or fixed (a thin wire bonded behind the front teeth), worn after braces or aligners to hold teeth in their new positions [1][2]. It protects the investment in a straighter smile: by limiting relapse, the tendency of teeth to drift back toward their old positions, a retainer keeps the alignment that treatment achieved. Relapse is attributed to recoil of periodontal fibres, pressure from lips, cheeks and tongue, the bite itself and continued growth, and Wikipedia describes it as a lifelong risk [2].

A Cochrane review of 15 randomised trials with 1,722 participants noted that teeth tend to drift back toward their original positions, so nearly everyone needs some form of retention, and that no agreed wear duration exists; some clinicians retain patients indefinitely [17]. Reviews of the orthodontic literature emphasise that retention should be planned in advance, may vary in duration, and depends on patient compliance, and that orthodontists are responsible for informing patients about the type and duration of retention even before active treatment starts [1].

Retainers come in removable and fixed families, each with variants for comfort, discretion and strength [1][2]. Wear schedules range from full-time to nights-only to part-time, set by the treating orthodontist, and many retainer wearers continue for years after treatment [2][17].

In looksmaxxing forums, retainers are discussed mainly in relation to whether wearing or stopping them affects jaw, palate or facial growth, whether a bonded wire harms facial structure, and whether they can be combined with mewing [6][7][8][9]. Orthodontic literature describes retainers as holding tooth position, and no published studies have tested effects on facial growth [1][2].

paras: After braces move teeth through bone, the surrounding tissues take time to reorganise around the new positions. Wikipedia lists four contributors to relapse: recoil of the periodontal fibres that anchor teeth, pressure from soft tissues, the occlusion (how the teeth meet), and continued growth [2]. Holding teeth still is what lets the fibres and bone adapt to the changed alignment [2].

The Cochrane review describes the near-universal tendency of teeth to move back toward their starting arrangement, which is why retention is usually part of the treatment plan, and notes that clinicians differ on how long it should last, with some advising retention indefinitely [17]. Wikipedia adds that irregular wear is a main cause of relapse with removable appliances [2]. Retainers are also used to treat some cases of overjet [2].
Retainers fall into removable and fixed families. Removable options are worn and taken out by the patient; fixed options stay in place and are checked at dental visits [1][2].

The Hawley retainer is a wire, usually crossing the six front teeth, attached to an acrylic plate that rests against the palate; it is one of the oldest designs and is named for Charles A. Hawley [2]. It is adjustable and robust, though it is more visible, can affect speech, may fracture, and holds lower incisors less well than vacuum-formed types [2]. A clear-wire version exists [2]. The 2023 critical review calls the passive Hawley-like appliances credible for maintaining occlusion and lists modifications: the Wrap Around, with a labial wire extending to the premolars, the translucent Astics, and a reinforced version with a metallic grid in the acrylic [1].

Vacuum-formed retainers are clear plastic trays moulded by heat and vacuum over a model of the teeth [2]. They are the most discreet and economical removable option, interfere less with speech, and hold lower incisors better than other removable types, but can crack in people who grind their teeth [2]. They are commonly worn overnight and removed for eating; wearing them while eating or inserting them straight after a sugary drink can trap food and sugars against the teeth [2]. The Cochrane review reported that thermoplastic retainers generally performed as well as or better than Hawley retainers, which broke more often and were more embarrassing for patients to wear [17].

The Begg retainer has a labial bow extending behind the last molar so the bite can settle; it is sturdy enough to wear while eating and is described as more retentive than a Hawley [2]. The Barrer or spring retainer has acrylic bows on both sides of the teeth and can correct minor relapse of the lower incisors; a version with cribs on the first molars reduces the risk of swallowing or aspirating it [2]. SMART retainer cases track wear, send reminders, reward use and can notify parents, and are aimed at improving compliance among teenagers [2].

A fixed retainer is a wire bonded to the back of the front teeth, usually a multistrand wire across all six front teeth or a round steel wire on the canines only [2]. Orthodontists use them where relapse is more likely, such as severe rotations, periodontal disease or a gap between the upper central incisors [2]. They need less patient cooperation but are harder to clean and can allow plaque to build up [2]. Direct-bonded retainers have been in clinical use since at least the 1970s [13], and trials have compared fixed designs and 3D-produced lingual retainers in laboratory tests [10][19].

Wikipedia notes that relapse is more likely when removable retainers are not worn consistently, that one cited review found Hawley retainers ineffective at preventing incisor crowding relapse, that vacuum-formed retainers appear better for lower incisors, and that fixed retainers gave the best retention [2].

The Cochrane review pooled trials comparing retainer types. It reported that thermoplastic removable retainers allowed slightly more lower-arch relapse than bonded multistrand wires, though the difference was small and the evidence low quality; removable retainers caused less gum bleeding, while patients found fixed retainers more acceptable to wear. It found no meaningful difference in failure between polyethylene ribbon and multistrand wire fixed retainers, and no difference in stability between full-time and part-time thermoplastic wear in one small trial. The authors concluded that higher-quality trials were needed before firm recommendations could be made [17].

Other trials have looked at adherence and cost. A randomised trial of 52 participants examined whether audiovisual instructions and weekly electronic reminders improved adherence to Hawley retainer wear and periodontal outcomes [4]. Cost and satisfaction comparisons of Hawley and vacuum-formed retainers [5], a cost-minimization analysis of an RCT of three retention methods [11] and a 3-year follow-up of various canine-to-canine retainers [14] have also been published.

Wikipedia says retainers should be worn as the orthodontist advises and cleaned gently with a soft brush and non-abrasive toothpaste or mild soap, kept dry and away from heat, and not soaked overnight [2]. Direct-bonded orthodontic retainers have been used clinically since at least the 1970s [13].

Removable retainers are cleaned before insertion with a wet toothbrush and non-abrasive toothpaste or mild soap, and retainer tablets are an alternative; fixed retainers are cleaned as part of the night-time routine [2]. Storage is dry, away from heat and sunlight, since very hot water can shrink them [2].

Poor cleaning can lead to plaque buildup, decay and gum inflammation, particularly with fixed retainers [2]. A systematic review describes "wire syndrome", unintended tooth movement that can occur even with an intact bonded retainer wire, as an undesirable event distinct from relapse, with functional and aesthetic complications [3].

Fixed retainers can detach or fracture, and removable ones can break, warp or be lost; the Barrer variant with molar cribs was designed partly to lower the chance of swallowing the appliance [2]. A 2023 laboratory study tested bond strength, discoloration and biodegradation of 3D-produced lingual retainers [19].

Forum threads on looksmax.org ask whether long-term retainer wear removes the chance of natural forward growth [6], whether a bonded retainer harms facial structure [7], whether to stop wearing a retainer [15][16], and whether retainers can be used to expand the palate or combined with mewing [8][9]. Posters also discuss whether plastic retainers shed micro-particles and whether they affect mandibular growth, with one replier pointing out that the retainer's purpose is to retain tooth position after braces [18]. Another thread asks about letting teeth shift to a particular look before abandoning a retainer [20].
Orthodontic literature describes retainers as maintaining tooth position, not as growth-modifying appliances [1][2].

Randomised trials compare retainer types for compliance, cost and clinical performance [4][5][10]. The Cochrane review of 15 trials covers stability, gum health and patient acceptance [17]. A randomised trial examined prefabricated thermoplastic retainers made with a virtual bracket removal technique [12], and a trial compared different fixed retainers [10]. A systematic review of bonded retainers documents wire syndrome as a complication [3]. No studies found on retainers affecting facial growth or appearance beyond tooth alignment.

lore.intro: Retainers are discussed on looksmax.org mostly as something that might help or hinder jaw and palate development.

claims.claim: Long-term retainer wear "kills" natural forward growth
claims.believers: A poster who had worn a retainer for about five years asked whether removing it could allow forward growth to resume [6].
claims.experts: Orthodontic reviews describe retainers as holding tooth position after treatment [1][2]; no studies test an effect on forward facial growth.

claims.claim: A retainer can expand the palate or be combined with mewing
claims.believers: Threads propose using a retainer to widen the palate or a custom "mewing retainer" [8][9].
claims.experts: Retainers are described as passive appliances for retention [1]; palate widening is done with dedicated expanders.

claims.claim: A bonded retainer harms facial structure
claims.believers: A poster asked whether a lingual bonded retainer is bad for facial structure and whether it should be removed [7].
claims.experts: Reviews list wire syndrome and plaque build-up as complications of bonded wires [2][3]; no published studies address facial structure.

claims.claim: Stopping the retainer lets teeth and jaw settle to a different look
claims.believers: Threads ask whether to stop wearing a retainer, including one poster considering cutting it to try a particular tooth look [15][16][20].
claims.experts: Orthodontic sources describe relapse as drift of teeth toward original positions, and some clinicians recommend indefinite retention [2][17].

claims.claim: Plastic retainers shed micro-particles or affect health
claims.believers: A poster who wore a retainer about 12 hours a day worried the plastic breaks off in the mouth [18].
claims.experts: Published retainer trials focus on stability, hygiene, cost and adherence; the 2023 3D-retainer study tested bond strength and biodegradation in the lab [19].

card.summary: The post-braces appliance that keeps teeth where they were moved; proven for retention, untested for jaw growth.
card.note: Bonded wires can cause unintended tooth movement; no evidence it changes facial growth.

quick.overview:
A retainer holds teeth in place after braces or aligners, either as a removable plastic or wire device or a wire bonded behind the teeth.
Its evidence is for keeping teeth aligned. Forum claims that retainers help or block jaw and palate growth have not been studied.
quick.mechanism: Passive pressure or a bonded wire keeps teeth from drifting back while surrounding fibres adapt.
quick.risks: Poor hygiene can cause decay or gum inflammation; bonded retainers can cause unwanted tooth movement (wire syndrome); removable ones can break or warp.

chain: Custom appliance holds teeth after braces or aligners
Resists drift back toward the old position
Straight, even smile stays in place
angle.text: A retainer keeps teeth in the straight alignment achieved by orthodontic treatment. Wearing it as the orthodontist advises is how patients keep crowding, gaps and rotations from returning.
